title: Review: pH curves; Buffers; Acid strength and molecular structure (AP)
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: AB07#t3 term and clue written for the game; AB10#t3 term and clue written for the game; AB07#t2 term and clue written for the game; AB10#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AB07#N.13, AB09#N.4b, AB10#N.11, AB07#N.9, AB09#N.6b, AB10#N.8, AB07#N.4b, AB09#N.13, AB10#N.4, AB07#N.12, AB09#N.11b, AB10#N.10. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Half-equivalence
items.clue: The stage of a titration at which [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.

items.label: Carboxylic acid
items.clue: A compound of the class R–COOH, in which only one hydrogen is donated.

items.label: Buffer region
items.clue: Gentle slope before the steep section, where HA and A⁻ are both present.

items.label: Inductive effect
items.clue: Atoms such as Cl pull electron density toward themselves through σ bonds.

questions.stem: Separate 20.0 mL portions of 0.100 M NaOH(aq) and of 0.100 M base B(aq) are each titrated with 0.100 M HCl(aq). Both need 20.0 mL of acid. Which feature of the curves shows that B is a weak base?

options.text: B's curve needs a larger volume of acid to reach its equivalence point than the NaOH curve does.
B's curve starts at a lower pH, falls gently at first, and reaches equivalence below pH 7.
B's curve has no steep section at all, because a weak base reacts with the acid only partly.
B's curve reaches its equivalence point above pH 7, because B is a base and so stays alkaline.

questions.stem: Equal volumes of the two solutions in each pair are mixed at 25°C. Which mixture is a buffer solution?

options.text: CH₃COOH, 0.10 M, and KOH, 0.10 M
HCl, 0.20 M, and NaCl, 0.10 M
CH₃COOH, 0.20 M, and NaOH, 0.10 M
HBr, 0.10 M, and KOH, 0.10 M

questions.explanation: The NaOH converts half the CH₃COOH to CH₃COO⁻, leaving large, equal concentrations of the weak acid and its conjugate base.

questions.stem: Four acids are each made up as 0.10 M solutions at 25°C: CH₃COOH, CH₃CH₂COOH, FCH₂COOH and BrCH₂COOH. Which solution has the lowest pH, and why?

options.text: CH₃CH₂COOH, because its longer carbon chain supplies more electron density to the –COOH group.
BrCH₂COOH, because Br is the largest of these atoms and so takes the negative charge itself.
FCH₂COOH, because F is the most electronegative and best stabilizes the conjugate base.
CH₃COOH, because without a halogen nothing holds back its acidic hydrogen atom.

questions.explanation: F pulls electron density away from –COO⁻ most strongly, spreading its charge. pKa: FCH₂COOH 2.59, the strongest acid here, so the lowest pH.

questions.stem: Which equation represents the equilibrium that determines the pH at the equivalence point of the titration of CH₃COOH(aq) with NaOH(aq)?

options.text: CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)
Na⁺(aq) + 2 H₂O(l) ⇌ NaOH(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)
H₂O(l) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COOH(aq) + OH⁻(aq)

questions.explanation: At the equivalence point the CH₃COOH has been converted to CH₃COO⁻. This conjugate base accepts protons from water, producing OH⁻, so this equilibrium sets the (basic) pH.

questions.stem: A buffer at 25°C contains 0.15 M NH₃ and 0.30 M NH₄Cl. The pKa of NH₄⁺ is 9.25. What is the pH of the buffer?
questions.explanation: NH₄⁺ is the acid, NH₃ the base: pH = 9.25 + log(0.15/0.30) = 9.25 − 0.30 = 8.95.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, and ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, both contain an O–H group. Ethanoic acid is a weak acid; ethanol does not measurably ionize in water. Which statement best explains the difference?

options.text: Ethanoic acid has more H atoms bonded to oxygen, so it has more protons to donate.
The O–H bond in ethanol is more polar, so its H atom is held more tightly.
Ethanol is a stronger base than water, so it takes H⁺ back as soon as it is lost.
In ethanoate the negative charge is shared over two O atoms by resonance.

questions.explanation: Delocalization stabilizes CH₃COO⁻. In CH₃CH₂O⁻ the charge sits on one O atom, so that ion forms far less readily.

questions.stem: A student titrates 25.0 mL of 0.10 M HA, a weak monoprotic acid, with 0.10 M NaOH and finds that the pH at the half-equivalence point is 4.70. The student then titrates 25.0 mL of 0.010 M HA with 0.010 M NaOH at the same temperature. How does the pH at the half-equivalence point of the second titration compare with that of the first?

options.text: It is higher by about one pH unit
It is higher by about half a pH unit
It is unchanged from the first titration
It is lower than in the first titration

questions.explanation: [HA] = [A⁻] at half-equivalence, so pH = pKa. Dilution changes both concentrations equally, and pKa is constant at a given temperature: still 4.70.

questions.stem: Inside cells, a buffer of dihydrogenphosphate ions, H₂PO₄⁻, and hydrogenphosphate ions, HPO₄²⁻, helps keep the pH close to 7. A process in the cell releases some OH⁻ ions. Which reaction removes most of the added OH⁻?

options.text: HPO₄²⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) → H₂PO₄⁻(aq)
H₂PO₄⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → HPO₄²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)
H₂PO₄⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) → H₃PO₄(aq)
HPO₄²⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → PO₄³⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)

questions.explanation: H₂PO₄⁻ is the weak acid of this pair, so it donates H⁺ to the OH⁻. The ratio [H₂PO₄⁻]/[HPO₄²⁻] changes only slightly, so the pH barely moves.

questions.stem: Hypochlorous acid, HClO, and hypoiodous acid, HIO, are both weak acids. Which choice identifies the stronger of the two acids and gives a correct reason?

options.text: HClO, because the H–Cl bond in HClO is more polar than the H–I bond in the molecule HIO
HIO, because acid strength increases down group 17, just as it does from HCl to HBr to HI
HClO, because Cl is more electronegative than I and stabilizes the conjugate base more
HIO, because the less electronegative I atom holds the electrons, and so the H atom, less tightly

questions.stem: A solution of a weak diprotic acid, H₂A, is titrated with NaOH(aq). The pH at the first equivalence point is 8.5. Which species, other than H₂O and Na⁺, is present at the highest concentration at the first equivalence point?

options.text: H₂A
A²⁻
OH⁻
HA⁻

questions.explanation: The OH⁻ added has removed one proton from every H₂A, so HA⁻ is the major species. Only small amounts of H₂A and A²⁻ form from it.

questions.stem: A buffer is made from CH₃COOH and NaCH₃COO. Which quantity sets the maximum amount of HCl that the buffer can neutralize before its pH begins to fall sharply?

options.text: The amount of CH₃COOH present
The pH of the buffer itself
The Ka of the acetic acid
The moles of CH₃COO⁻ present

questions.explanation: Added H₃O⁺ reacts with CH₃COO⁻ 1 : 1, so the moles of CH₃COO⁻ set how much HCl the buffer can neutralize.

questions.stem: HBr is a strong acid. A student dissolves KBr(s) in pure water at 25°C to make a 0.10 M solution; the K⁺ ion does not react with water. Which prediction of the pH of the solution, with its reason, is correct?

options.text: Close to 13, because the conjugate base of a strong acid is itself a strong base
Equal to 7, because Br⁻ is too weak a base to remove H⁺ ions from water molecules
Slightly above 7, because an ion with a negative charge pulls H⁺ ions out of water
Slightly below 7, because Br⁻ comes from the acid HBr and keeps some of its acidity

questions.explanation: Br⁻ is so stable that it has a negligible tendency to accept a proton. Neither ion reacts with water, so the pH is 7 at 25°C.
